description: One of the largest land predators ever, with a massive skull, bone-crushing teeth the size of bananas, and surprisingly tiny two-fingered arms. It ruled the floodplains of western North America at the very end of the age of dinosaurs.
interestingFacts: Its bite was the strongest of any land animal ever measured — over 5 tonnes of force.
Despite its size, some scientists think it could jog at around 20 km/h.
A famous specimen named Sue is the most complete T. rex ever found.

description: A tank-like plant-eater with two long brow horns, a shorter nose horn, and a huge bony neck frill. It lived alongside Tyrannosaurus rex and could defend itself against it.
interestingFacts: Its skull could be over 2.5 metres long — one of the largest of any land animal.
It sheared through tough plants with hundreds of teeth stacked in batteries.
Fossils show healed horn injuries, evidence of real battles.

imageAttribution: Fred Wierum, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0
description: A fast, feathered hunter about the size of a turkey — much smaller than in the movies. It used a large sickle-shaped claw on each foot to pin down its prey in the deserts of Mongolia.
interestingFacts: A famous fossil preserves one locked in combat with a Protoceratops.
Quill knobs on its arm bones prove it had feathers.
Its sickle claw could grow to about 6.5 cm long.

imageAttribution: Fred Wierum, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0
description: Instantly recognisable by the two rows of big bony plates along its back and the four long tail spikes it swung at attackers. Its brain was famously tiny — about the size of a walnut.
interestingFacts: The spiky tail weapon is nicknamed the 'thagomizer'.
Its back plates may have flushed with blood to change colour.
An Allosaurus fossil has a wound matching a Stegosaurus tail spike.

imageAttribution: Dmitry Bogdanov, Wikimedia Commons, Public domain
description: A giraffe-like giant whose front legs were longer than its back legs, tilting its long neck up to browse treetops other dinosaurs couldn't reach — up to 9 metres above the ground.
interestingFacts: It's named 'arm lizard' because of those long front legs.
It swallowed leaves whole — no chewing — and let its stomach do the work.
It was the first dinosaur shown in the movie Jurassic Park.

description: One of the longest dinosaurs known from good skeletons, built like a suspension bridge with a whip-like tail longer than its neck. Casts of its skeleton stand in museums all over the world.
interestingFacts: Its tail had about 80 vertebrae and may have cracked like a whip.
It likely stripped leaves from branches with comb-like front teeth.
Steel tycoon Andrew Carnegie funded the famous specimen 'Dippy'.

description: Longer than T. rex, with a crocodile-like snout for catching fish and a spectacular 1.7-metre sail on its back. It's the best candidate we have for a swimming dinosaur.
interestingFacts: The original fossils were destroyed in a WWII bombing raid on Munich.
New fossils show it had a tall paddle-like tail for swimming.
Its nostrils sat high on its skull, handy for a life around water.

imageAttribution: Emily Willoughby, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0
description: A living fortress covered in bony armour plates, with a huge club of solid bone at the end of its tail that could swing hard enough to break a predator's leg.
interestingFacts: Even its eyelids had bony armour.
The tail club could weigh more than 20 kilograms.
It kept its soft belly close to the ground — flipping it over was the only way in.

description: The top predator of the Late Jurassic, with short horns above its eyes and a mouth that opened extremely wide. It hunted the great plant-eaters of its time, possibly in groups.
interestingFacts: More than 46 individuals were found in one Utah quarry alone.
It may have used its upper jaw like a hatchet to slash prey.
It lived 80 million years before T. rex — they never met.

description: A duck-billed dinosaur with a long, curved tube of bone sweeping back from its head. The hollow crest worked like a trombone, letting it make deep honking calls across the herd.
interestingFacts: Scientists have recreated its call with computer models — a low foghorn sound.
The crest could be over 1 metre long.
It could walk on two legs or four.

description: A heavyweight cousin of Diplodocus with a thicker, more powerful build. For a century it was better known by its other name — Brontosaurus, the 'thunder lizard'.
interestingFacts: Its neck bones were unusually wide and strong — maybe for neck-wrestling contests.
A single thigh bone can be taller than an adult human.
The Brontosaurus name was recently argued back to life for a close relative.

description: One of the very first dinosaurs ever named, famous for the sharp thumb spikes it used like daggers. Dozens of complete skeletons were found together deep in a Belgian coal mine.
interestingFacts: Early scientists thought its thumb spike was a horn on its nose.
It was only the second creature ever called a 'dinosaur'.
It could grip branches with a bendy little finger.

description: The famous head-butting dinosaur, with a domed skull roof up to 25 centimetres thick surrounded by a crown of bony knobs. Rivals may have rammed each other like bighorn sheep.
interestingFacts: Its skull dome was 20 times thicker than a human skull.
Some skulls show healed injuries from head-on collisions.
Young ones had flat heads that domed as they grew.

imageAttribution: Fred Wierum, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0
description: A South American sprinter with two devil-like horns over its eyes and arms even stubbier than T. rex's. Its huge leg muscles made it one of the fastest big predators ever.
interestingFacts: Skin impressions show it was covered in rows of scaly bumps.
Its arms were so short they had almost no use at all.
It may have sprinted at over 50 km/h.

imageAttribution: Connor Ashbridge, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0
description: An early predator wearing two thin, rounded crests on its head like a double mohawk. The real animal was much bigger than the movies show — and there's no evidence it spat venom.
interestingFacts: It was the largest land predator of its time in North America.
The movie frill and venom were pure fiction.
Its fossils were found on Navajo Nation land in Arizona.

description: A chicken-sized speedster that chased lizards and insects across Jurassic lagoon islands. For over a century it held the record as the smallest known dinosaur.
interestingFacts: One fossil still has a whole lizard inside its stomach.
It lived on the same islands where Archaeopteryx flew.
Its name means 'elegant jaw' for its delicate skull.

description: The raptor that changed science: its build convinced researchers that dinosaurs were fast, warm-blooded and bird-like. The Jurassic Park 'Velociraptors' were really modelled on it.
interestingFacts: Its study kick-started the 'dinosaur renaissance' of the 1960s.
Several skeletons found together hint that it hunted in packs.
Its killing claw stayed razor-sharp by never touching the ground.

description: Possibly the largest land animal that ever lived — as heavy as ten elephants. It's known from just a few colossal bones, including vertebrae taller than a person.
interestingFacts: A single backbone vertebra measures 1.6 metres tall.
Hatchlings the size of a cat grew 25,000 times heavier as adults.
It was discovered by a rancher who thought a bone was petrified wood.

description: The dinosaur with the longest claws of any animal ever — up to a metre each. Despite the terrifying scythes, this pot-bellied giant used them to hook leafy branches, not prey.
interestingFacts: Scientists first thought its claws belonged to a giant turtle.
Its claws could reach 1 metre — the longest of any known animal.
It was a plant-eater descended from meat-eating ancestors.

description: The punk rocker of horned dinosaurs: four to six long spikes fanned out from its frill, with a half-metre horn on its nose. The display probably impressed rivals and mates alike.
interestingFacts: Its nose horn alone could be 57 centimetres long.
Huge bone beds show its herds numbered in the hundreds.
Each individual's frill spikes were arranged slightly differently.

description: A duck-billed dinosaur with a tall, rounded crest like an ancient Greek helmet. Air looping through the hollow crest gave each animal its own deep, resonant voice.
interestingFacts: One fossil preserved skin impressions over much of the body.
Its crest shape changed with age and differed between sexes.
It had up to 600 tiny teeth for grinding plants.

imageAttribution: Connor Ashbridge, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0
description: A Jurassic predator with a blade-like horn on its nose, small horns over its eyes, and a row of little armour plates down its back — unique among meat-eaters.
interestingFacts: It's the only known meat-eater with bony armour along its spine.
Its teeth were enormous for its body size.
It competed with the bigger Allosaurus for the same prey.

description: A fish-hunting cousin of Spinosaurus found in an English clay pit, named for the huge 31-centimetre claw on each thumb. Its crocodile-like jaws held nearly a hundred teeth.
interestingFacts: Fish scales and a young Iguanodon were found in its stomach.
It was discovered by an amateur fossil hunter, a plumber named William Walker.
It's one of the most complete big predators ever found in Britain.

description: A sheep-sized early relative of Triceratops with a bony frill but no big horns. Whole herds, nests and even eggs were found preserved in Mongolia's Gobi Desert sands.
interestingFacts: Its skeletons may have inspired the legend of the griffin.
A famous fossil shows one frozen mid-fight with a Velociraptor.
Dozens were found in every size from hatchling to adult.

description: A slender, fast-running early predator with a long neck and tail and needle-sharp teeth. One of the earliest dinosaurs, it hunted small animals in herds across the deserts of ancient North America.
interestingFacts: Hundreds of skeletons were found jumbled together at Ghost Ranch, New Mexico.
It was one of the earliest true dinosaurs, from near the dawn of the age of dinosaurs.
A Coelophysis skull flew aboard Space Shuttle Endeavour in 1998.

description: A large early plant-eater that reared up on its hind legs to browse high foliage. An ancestor-type of the giant long-necked sauropods, it was one of the first big dinosaurs.
interestingFacts: It was one of the very first dinosaurs ever scientifically named, back in the 1830s.
Dozens of skeletons have been dug from European 'dinosaur graveyards'.
It walked on two legs but had a long neck and small head like its giant sauropod cousins.

description: A stocky long-necked giant with a short, boxy skull and large nostrils above its eyes. It was the most common sauropod of the Jurassic plains of western North America.
interestingFacts: Its name means 'chambered lizard' after the hollow, air-filled chambers in its backbone.
It is the most complete and commonly found sauropod from the Morrison Formation.
Its spoon-shaped teeth were strong enough to chew tough plants whole.

description: A colossal Chinese sauropod famous for having one of the longest necks of any animal that has ever lived — almost half of its entire body length.
interestingFacts: Its neck could reach up to about 15 metres — the longest neck known in the animal kingdom.
The neck alone made up nearly half of its total body length.
It was named after Mamen Brook in China, where the first bones were found.

description: A huge duck-billed dinosaur with hundreds of grinding teeth packed into its jaws. It lived in vast herds right up to the very end of the age of dinosaurs, alongside T. rex.
interestingFacts: Its jaws held a 'dental battery' of up to a thousand teeth for grinding tough plants.
Mummified specimens have preserved its skin texture and even a fleshy head crest.
It lived side by side with Tyrannosaurus rex and was likely its prey.

description: A duck-billed plant-eater crowned with a hollow, hatchet-shaped crest on its head. The crest was filled with air tubes that may have let it trumpet loud calls.
interestingFacts: Its hollow head crest was shaped like a hatchet or axe blade.
Air passages inside the crest may have worked like a trumpet to make sounds.
It was named in honour of Canadian palaeontologist Lawrence Lambe.

description: An African cousin of Stegosaurus with a double row of plates near the shoulders that gave way to a fearsome set of long, sharp spikes down its back and tail.
interestingFacts: Unlike Stegosaurus, most of its back and tail were lined with spikes rather than plates.
It had extra spikes jutting out from its shoulders or hips for defence.
Its fossils were found in Tanzania, in East Africa.

description: A duck-billed dinosaur whose nesting grounds revealed that it cared for its babies. Whole colonies nested together, tending eggs and feeding hatchlings in the nest.
interestingFacts: Its name means 'good mother lizard' — the first clear proof dinosaurs cared for their young.
Fossil nesting colonies were found with eggs, babies and adults together.
It is the official state fossil of Montana, USA.

description: A feathered, parrot-beaked dinosaur that was wrongly accused of stealing eggs. We now know the 'stolen' eggs were its own — it was actually sitting on its nest like a bird.
interestingFacts: It was named 'egg thief' by mistake — it was really protecting its own nest.
It had a toothless beak and a crest on its head, a bit like a cassowary.
Fossils show it brooded its eggs the same way modern birds do.

description: An ostrich-like dinosaur with a toothless beak, long legs and feathered arms. Built for speed, it could sprint away from predators across the open plains.
interestingFacts: It looked and ran much like a modern ostrich and may have reached 50–70 km/h.
Fossils show wing-like feathers on its arms even though it couldn't fly.
Its toothless beak suggests it ate plants, insects and small animals.

description: A crow-sized creature that is half dinosaur, half bird — with feathers and wings but also teeth, clawed fingers and a long bony tail. It is one of the most famous fossils ever found.
interestingFacts: It is often called the 'first bird' and links dinosaurs to modern birds.
It had feathers and wings like a bird but teeth and a bony tail like a dinosaur.
Its fossils were found in Germany just after Darwin published his theory of evolution.

description: A lighter, faster relative of T. rex that ruled Canada a few million years earlier. It had the same tiny arms and huge jaws, but a slimmer, speedier build.
interestingFacts: It was a smaller, older cousin of Tyrannosaurus rex.
A bonebed of 26 individuals hints that it may have hunted in packs.
Being lighter than T. rex, it was probably a faster runner.

description: A small, parrot-beaked plant-eater that was an early cousin of Triceratops — long before the great horned dinosaurs evolved. It is one of the best-known dinosaurs of all.
interestingFacts: Its parrot-like beak gives it the name 'parrot lizard'.
It was an early relative of the horned dinosaurs like Triceratops.
One superb fossil preserves bristles on its tail and even its camouflage colours.

description: The Asian cousin of T. rex and the top predator of Cretaceous Mongolia. It shared the same giant jaws and comically tiny two-fingered arms.
interestingFacts: It was the largest predator in Asia at the end of the age of dinosaurs.
It is the closest known relative of Tyrannosaurus rex.
Like T. rex, it had huge jaws but very short, small arms.

description: One of the largest meat-eating dinosaurs ever, with blade-like teeth serrated like a shark's. It prowled the rivers of North Africa alongside Spinosaurus.
interestingFacts: Its name means 'shark-toothed lizard' after its serrated, blade-like teeth.
It rivalled T. rex and Spinosaurus as one of the biggest land predators ever.
Its original fossils were destroyed when a museum was bombed in World War II.

description: A huge predator with tall spines along its back forming a low ridge or sail. It was the apex hunter of early Cretaceous North America.
interestingFacts: Tall spines along its backbone formed a muscular ridge down its back.
It was the top predator of its time and place in North America.
Fossil trackways seem to show it stalking a giant long-necked sauropod.

description: One of the strangest dinosaurs of all — a giant, humpbacked, duck-billed ostrich-dinosaur. For 50 years it was known only from its enormous 2.4-metre arms.
interestingFacts: For half a century it was a mystery known only from two gigantic arms.
Its arms were about 2.4 metres long — some of the largest of any predator.
The full skeleton revealed a bizarre humped back and a duck-like bill.

description: A giant feathered, beaked dinosaur as long as a bus — a super-sized relative of the little Oviraptor. It shows that some bird-like dinosaurs grew to enormous size.
interestingFacts: It was a bird-like beaked dinosaur that grew as big as a Tyrannosaurus.
It was around 35 times heavier than its close feathered relatives.
Despite its size it had a toothless beak and probably feathers.

description: One of the earliest dinosaurs of all, from a time when dinosaurs were still rare. This nimble predator had grasping hands and a special sliding jaw joint to grip struggling prey.
interestingFacts: It is one of the oldest known dinosaurs, over 230 million years old.
It lived when dinosaurs were still a small part of the animal world.
A flexible sliding jaw joint helped it hold onto wriggling prey.

description: A living tank covered head to tail in bony armour — even its eyelids were shielded with bone. A heavy club at the end of its tail could smash an attacker's legs.
interestingFacts: It was so well armoured that even its eyelids had bony shields.
Its tail ended in a heavy club of solid bone for swinging at predators.
It is one of the best-known armoured dinosaurs, with many skeletons found.

description: A spiky armoured dinosaur bristling with blade-like spikes along its sides and a shield of fused bone over its hips. It relied on armour, not speed, to survive.
interestingFacts: Rows of flat, blade-like spikes ran along each side of its body.
A shield of fused bony plates protected its hips.
Many individuals were found buried together in Utah.

description: A strange long-necked plant-eater with a wide, straight-edged mouth packed with hundreds of tiny teeth — like a living lawn-mower that grazed low plants.
interestingFacts: Its wide mouth held more than 500 tiny teeth arranged like a comb.
It replaced each tooth about once a month as they wore out.
Its skull was so full of air spaces it was almost see-through.

description: A powerful Jurassic hunter from England that holds a special place in history: it was the very first dinosaur ever given a scientific name.
interestingFacts: It was the first dinosaur ever scientifically named, back in 1824.
It was one of the fossils that inspired the invention of the word 'dinosaur'.
Early scientists wrongly pictured it as a giant four-legged lizard.

description: A sturdy plant-eater with a horny beak that could walk on two legs or drop to all fours to feed. It was an early relative of the famous Iguanodon.
interestingFacts: It was a close relative and forerunner of Iguanodon.
It could switch between walking on two legs and four.
It cropped plants with a toothless beak and chewed with cheek teeth.

description: One of the largest predators of the Jurassic, armed with long dagger-like teeth. It hunted across what is now North America and Europe.
interestingFacts: It was among the biggest meat-eaters of the entire Jurassic Period.
Fossils from Portugal make it one of Europe's largest known land predators.
It had exceptionally long, blade-like teeth for its size.

description: One of Australia's most complete dinosaurs, a big plant-eater with a strange hollow bump on its snout that may have been used to make loud honking calls.
interestingFacts: It is one of the most complete dinosaur skeletons ever found in Australia.
A hollow bump on its snout may have amplified its calls.
It could walk on two legs or four while browsing plants.

description: A medium-sized Spanish predator with a bizarre tall triangular hump in front of its hips, and bumps on its arms that hint it may have had quill-like structures.
interestingFacts: It had a strange tall, triangular hump rising just in front of its hips.
Bumps on its arm bones suggest it may have had quill-like feathers.
Its beautifully preserved skeleton was found in Spain.

description: The first meat-eating dinosaur ever discovered in Antarctica, sporting an odd crest that swept across its head above the eyes.
interestingFacts: It was the first meat-eating dinosaur found in Antarctica.
Its curled head crest earned it the nickname 'Elvisaurus'.
When it lived, Antarctica was warmer and covered in forests.

description: A bulldog-snouted predator from Madagascar with a single stubby horn on its head and tiny useless arms. It is one of the few dinosaurs with solid evidence it ate its own kind.
interestingFacts: It had a short, deep bulldog-like snout with a small horn on top.
Bite marks on its own bones are strong evidence that it was a cannibal.
Its arms were even shorter and more useless than those of T. rex.

description: A large tyrannosaur relative covered in shaggy feathers — the biggest feathered dinosaur ever found. It proved that even giant meat-eaters could be fuzzy.
interestingFacts: It is the largest dinosaur ever found with direct evidence of feathers.
Its body was covered in long, hair-like filament feathers.
It showed that big tyrannosaur relatives could be fluffy, not scaly.

description: One of the earliest and most primitive of the plated stegosaurs, from China. Unlike its later cousins, it still had small teeth at the front of its mouth.
interestingFacts: It is one of the oldest and most primitive stegosaurs known.
Unlike later stegosaurs, it kept small teeth at the front of its beak.
A pair of large spikes stuck out from its shoulders.

description: One of the earliest and most complete armoured dinosaurs, covered in rows of bony studs. It sits near the root of the family tree that led to Stegosaurus and Ankylosaurus.
interestingFacts: It is one of the earliest and most completely known armoured dinosaurs.
Rows of bony scutes ran along its back and sides for protection.
It was an early relative of both the plated and club-tailed armoured dinosaurs.

description: A small, speedy two-legged plant-eater built like a gazelle of the dinosaur world, darting away from danger on the ancient Isle of Wight.
interestingFacts: It was a small, fast runner that relied on speed to escape predators.
Scientists once wrongly believed it climbed trees like a modern bird.
Its ridged teeth sharpened themselves as it chewed tough plants.

description: A small bone-headed dinosaur with a thick, domed skull. A cousin of Pachycephalosaurus, it may have used its reinforced head for shoving contests or display.
interestingFacts: It had a thick, bony dome on top of its skull.
It was a smaller relative of the famous Pachycephalosaurus.
Its reinforced skull may have been used for head-shoving or display.

description: Possibly the earliest known dinosaur — or its closest cousin — from the Middle Triassic of Tanzania. Living around 245 million years ago, it pushes the dawn of the dinosaurs back by millions of years.
interestingFacts: It may be the oldest known dinosaur, living about 245 million years ago.
It is named after Lake Nyasa (Lake Malawi), near where its bones were found in Tanzania.
Its fossils sat in a museum drawer for roughly 80 years before being identified in 2012.

description: A colossal long-necked titanosaur, one of the very last giant sauropods in North America and among the largest animals ever to walk the continent.
interestingFacts: It was one of the biggest dinosaurs ever found in North America.
It was among the last giant long-necked dinosaurs before the extinction.
Like other titanosaurs, it may have had bony armour studs in its skin.

description: A tiny, four-winged feathered dinosaur about the size of a crow — one of the closest known relatives of the very first birds.
interestingFacts: It had feathers on all four limbs, like a second pair of wings.
It was the first dinosaur to have its full body colour worked out — grey with a reddish crest.
It lived slightly before the famous 'first bird' Archaeopteryx.

description: A tall, feathered, beaked dinosaur with a crest on its head, nicknamed the 'chicken from hell'. It roamed North America right up to the extinction.
interestingFacts: Scientists nicknamed it 'the chicken from hell'.
It had a toothless beak, a bony head crest and a feathered body.
It was one of the largest oviraptorosaurs from North America.

description: One of the largest raptors ever discovered, from South America — with a long, low crocodile-like snout and surprisingly short arms for a dromaeosaur.
interestingFacts: It was one of the biggest raptor dinosaurs known, up to ~5.5 m long.
Its arms were unusually short for a raptor.
Its long, cone-toothed snout suggests it caught fish.

description: The best-preserved armoured dinosaur ever found — nicknamed the 'sleeping dragon' — with its skin, armour and even its last meal fossilised in stunning detail.
interestingFacts: It is so well preserved it looks almost like a statue of a living animal.
Its preserved colour shows reddish camouflage, darker on top and lighter below.
Its fossilised stomach revealed the ferns it ate for its last meal.

description: One of the most famous dinosaurs of all — a huge, long-necked, whip-tailed giant of the Jurassic plains whose very name means 'thunder lizard'.
interestingFacts: Its name means 'thunder lizard'.
For a long time it was thought to be the same as Apatosaurus, but it was reinstated as its own kind in 2015.
It had a long whip-like tail and a small head far from its body.

description: A peacock-sized feathered dinosaur with a showy fan of feathers on its tail and arms — clear evidence that many dinosaurs were feathered.
interestingFacts: It had a fan of feathers on its tail and short arms.
It was about the size of a peacock.
It swallowed small stones to help grind up its food.

description: A large crested oviraptorid famous for spectacular fossils that show it sitting on its nest, arms spread over the eggs, exactly like a brooding bird.
interestingFacts: Fossils show it brooding its nest just like a modern bird.
It had a tall head crest and a toothless beak.
A famous specimen is nicknamed 'Big Mama'.

description: A large, lightly-built predator with enormous sickle-shaped hand claws — which were first mistaken for the foot claws of a giant raptor.
interestingFacts: It was named for a huge 35 cm claw that was first thought to be a foot claw — but it grew on its hand.
It had long arms and a slender build.
It gives its name to a whole group of predators, the megaraptorans.

description: A horned dinosaur with an oversized nose and long, forward-curving brow horns that look remarkably like the horns of a modern cow.
interestingFacts: It had long forward-curving horns like a cow's.
It also had an unusually big nose.
It lived on the ancient island continent of Laramidia.

description: A rugged horned dinosaur that swapped the usual nose horn for a massive slab of bone, and roamed the far north in huge herds — even inside the Arctic Circle.
interestingFacts: Instead of a nose horn it had a thick slab of bone called a boss.
Huge herds lived in the cold, dark Arctic.
It starred in the film 'Walking with Dinosaurs'.

description: One of the largest land animals of all time — a titanosaur so enormous that a full-size cast of its skeleton barely fits inside a museum hall.
interestingFacts: It was up to about 37 m long, among the biggest animals ever.
It weighed as much as roughly ten elephants.
A cast of its skeleton is too long to fit in a single room.

description: One of the most completely known titanosaurs, from Madagascar — including a rare, near-complete skull that revealed what these giants' heads looked like.
interestingFacts: It is one of the most complete titanosaurs ever found.
A fossil baby shows they grew fast and looked like miniature adults.
It is named after Rapeto, a giant from Malagasy folklore.

description: A comparatively small sauropod that carried its own body armour — bony plates set into its skin — proving that even long-necked giants could be armoured.
interestingFacts: It had bony armour plates embedded in its skin.
It surprised scientists, who didn't expect armoured sauropods.
It nested together in large breeding colonies.

description: One of the longest animals that has ever lived — a diplodocid whose neck and whip-like tail stretched its body out to some 35 metres or more.
interestingFacts: It may have been over 35 m long, one of the longest dinosaurs ever.
Its tail could probably crack like a whip.
Its name simply means 'super lizard'.

description: One of the largest of all the plated stegosaurs, and the very first stegosaur ever discovered — armed with sharp spikes running down its back and tail.
interestingFacts: It was the first stegosaur ever discovered, in 1875.
It was one of the largest stegosaurs, heavier than Stegosaurus.
Sharp spikes, rather than broad plates, lined much of its back.

description: A small, lightly-built plant-eater built for speed, dashing across the Jurassic plains to escape predators like Allosaurus.
interestingFacts: It was a fast runner on long, slender legs.
It had no front teeth — just a horny cropping beak.
Speed was its main defence against big predators.

description: A heavily armoured nodosaur bristling with bony plates and large forward-pointing shoulder spikes, but with no tail club.
interestingFacts: It had big forward-pointing spikes on its shoulders.
Rival males may have used the spikes to shove each other.
Unlike ankylosaurs, it had no bony tail club.

description: A dwarf sauropod, only about six metres long — a giant's family shrunk down to size by life on a small prehistoric island.
interestingFacts: It was a dwarf sauropod, tiny for its family at about 6 m long.
It shrank because it lived on a small island with limited food.
It is a textbook example of 'island dwarfism'.

description: A duck-billed dinosaur easily known by the tall, arched 'Roman nose' bump on its snout, which may have been used for display or head-butting.
interestingFacts: It is named for its distinctive arched, hooked nose.
The nose bump may have been used to signal or shove rivals.
Skin impressions show it had pebbly, scaly hide.

description: A cat-sized early plant-eater with an unusual mouth: three different kinds of teeth, including a pair of little tusks.
interestingFacts: It had three different types of teeth, which is very rare in dinosaurs.
It sported a pair of small tusks, perhaps for display or fighting.
It was only about the size of a house cat.

description: One of the oldest known tyrannosaurs — a stocky predator with a short, wide skull and forward-facing eyes that gave it excellent 3-D vision.
interestingFacts: It is one of the earliest known tyrannosaurs, about 80 million years old.
Its name means 'gore king'.
Its wide skull gave it overlapping, binocular vision like T. rex.

description: A tyrannosaur that lived inside the ancient Arctic Circle, smaller than T. rex — perhaps shrunk to survive the long, dark, food-poor polar winters.
interestingFacts: It lived in the freezing, dark Arctic.
It was smaller than T. rex, maybe to cope with scarce winter food.
Its name means 'polar bear lizard' in the Iñupiaq language.

description: A graceful duck-billed dinosaur from the Russian Far East, crowned with a huge, fan-shaped hollow crest and a long, swan-like neck.
interestingFacts: It had a big hatchet- or fan-shaped crest on its head.
Its name means 'giant swan' for its long neck.
It is one of the most complete duckbills found outside the Americas.

description: A large duck-billed dinosaur with a bony spike-like crest sweeping back from its head — and one of the few dinosaurs known from both North America and Asia.
interestingFacts: It had a backward-pointing spike crest on its skull.
It is known from both North America and Mongolia.
The crest may have supported a colourful skin flap for display.

description: Possibly the tallest dinosaur of all — a towering cousin of Brachiosaurus that could lift its head as high as a six-storey building.
interestingFacts: It could raise its head about 17 m up — as tall as a six-storey building.
It is known mostly from four gigantic neck bones.
It was an even taller relative of Brachiosaurus.

description: A medium-sized plant-eater with an extraordinarily long, stiff tail — and the animal most often found alongside the fearsome raptor Deinonychus.
interestingFacts: Its long, stiff tail made up more than half its length.
Its bones are often found with teeth of the raptor Deinonychus.
It may have been a favourite prey of pack-hunting raptors.

description: The top predator of Jurassic China — a big-headed, Allosaurus-like hunter that stalked giant long-necked dinosaurs like Mamenchisaurus.
interestingFacts: It was the apex predator of Jurassic China.
It looked and lived much like the North American Allosaurus.
It hunted huge long-necked dinosaurs.

description: A superbly preserved club-tailed ankylosaur named after the movie monster it resembles, complete with fossilised armour and skin.
interestingFacts: It is named after the demon Zuul from the film Ghostbusters.
Its species name means 'destroyer of shins', for its heavy tail club.
It was preserved with armour and even skin intact.

description: A slender, long-snouted southern raptor about the size of a chicken, and a small cousin of the much larger Austroraptor.
interestingFacts: It had a long, low snout full of tiny teeth.
Its teeth lacked the usual steak-knife serrations.
It was a small relative of the giant raptor Austroraptor.

description: An early horned dinosaur with two large curving spikes rising from its frill like a pair of devil's horns.
interestingFacts: Two big curved spikes on its frill look like devil horns.
It is one of the oldest horned dinosaurs of its group.
Its name means 'devil horned face'.

description: One of the very first dinosaurs ever named — an early armoured plant-eater whose spiky body helped define what a 'dinosaur' even was.
interestingFacts: It was one of the first three dinosaurs ever named, in 1833.
It helped define the original meaning of the word 'Dinosauria'.
Rows of bony spikes ran along its body.

description: A lighter, more slender relative of Iguanodon and one of the best-known dinosaurs from England's Isle of Wight.
interestingFacts: It was a slimmer, lighter cousin of Iguanodon.
It is named after Gideon Mantell, who discovered Iguanodon.
It is one of the most complete dinosaurs found in Britain.

description: A giant shark-toothed predator with, surprisingly, tiny T. rex-like arms — showing that different huge hunters shrank their arms independently.
interestingFacts: It is named after a dragon from Game of Thrones.
It was a giant predator with tiny arms, just like T. rex.
Its tiny arms evolved separately from those of T. rex.

description: A slender, fast, feathered desert runner with strange stubby arms — each ending in a single powerful claw, probably used to rip open insect nests.
interestingFacts: Each tiny arm ended in a single stout claw.
It likely dug into termite or ant nests like an anteater.
It was long-legged, fast and covered in feathers.

description: A spiky British armoured dinosaur with a fearsome array of spines over its neck and shoulders and a solid shield of bone across its hips.
interestingFacts: Large spikes guarded its neck and shoulders.
A shield of fused bone covered its hips.
It is one of Britain's best-known armoured dinosaurs.

description: A bone-headed dinosaur whose smooth, rounded dome was ringed with a row of small bony spikes and bumps.
interestingFacts: Its rounded skull dome was ringed with little spikes.
It was a relative of the famous Pachycephalosaurus.
The dome may have been used for display or shoving matches.

description: A stocky, single-horned predator and one of the few dinosaurs known from India, where it hunted the long-necked giants of the Narmada valley.
interestingFacts: It is one of the few dinosaurs known from India.
It had a single low horn on top of its head.
It hunted the sauropods of ancient India.

description: One of the earliest armoured dinosaurs — yet small and light enough to run on two legs, wearing hundreds of tiny bony studs down its back.
interestingFacts: It was an early armoured dinosaur that could run on two legs.
Hundreds of little bony studs covered its back.
It was a distant ancestor-type of Stegosaurus and Ankylosaurus.

description: A horned dinosaur whose fossils were forgotten in a museum drawer for around 90 years before anyone realised they belonged to a brand-new species.
interestingFacts: Its bones sat unstudied in a museum for about 90 years.
Its frill was decorated with forward-curling hooks and spikes.
Its name means 'spine face'.

description: A close relative of Triceratops with one of the largest skulls of any land animal ever — a gigantic frill pierced by two huge openings.
interestingFacts: It had one of the largest skulls of any land animal, up to ~2.6 m long.
Its enormous frill had two big holes in it.
It lived right alongside Triceratops.

description: A big-frilled horned dinosaur whose short brow horns pointed out sideways rather than forward, discovered in the badlands of southern Utah.
interestingFacts: Its brow horns stuck out sideways instead of forward.
It lived on the island continent of Laramidia.
It was found in the badlands of southern Utah.

imageAttribution: Dmitry Bogdanov, Wikimedia Commons, Public domain
description: One of the largest land predators ever discovered, a carcharodontosaurid from Patagonia that rivalled or slightly exceeded Tyrannosaurus in length. It had a long, low skull filled with blade-like teeth built for slicing flesh from giant sauropod prey.
interestingFacts: Slightly longer than Tyrannosaurus rex, though more lightly built.
Named after Rubén Carolini, who discovered it in Patagonia in 1993.
Its thin, blade-like teeth were suited to slashing flesh rather than crushing bone.

imageAttribution: Fred Wierum, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0
description: A small sauropod instantly recognisable for the tall, forked double row of spines running along its neck and back. These may have supported twin sails, a mane, or served for display and defence.
interestingFacts: Its neck bore two parallel rows of tall spines unlike any other sauropod.
The spines may have carried sails or a keratin sheath for display or defence.
Tiny for a sauropod at only about 10 metres long.

description: One of the largest of the ostrich-like ornithomimids, a lightly built, long-legged runner with a toothless beak. It roamed the Late Cretaceous floodplains of the Gobi, likely feeding on plants, small animals and eggs.
interestingFacts: One of the largest 'ostrich dinosaurs' ever found.
Its long, slender legs suggest it was a very fast runner.
Featured in Jurassic Park's famous flocking stampede scene.

imageAttribution: Fred Wierum, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0
description: A crow-sized dromaeosaur from the Jehol Biota with long flight feathers on all four limbs — in effect, four wings. Preserved pigment structures show it had glossy, iridescent black plumage.
interestingFacts: Had feathered 'wings' on both its arms and its legs — four in total.
Fossilised pigment shows its feathers were glossy, iridescent black.
One of the smallest known dinosaurs, roughly the size of a crow.

description: An early, small-bodied tyrannosauroid from the Late Jurassic of China — one of the oldest known relatives of Tyrannosaurus. It carried a tall, thin, ornamental crest along the top of its snout.
interestingFacts: An early cousin of T. rex that lived roughly 90 million years before it.
Bore a tall but fragile head crest, almost certainly for display.
Its name means 'crown dragon', after that distinctive crest.

description: A small, bird-like troodontid with large, forward-facing eyes and one of the highest brain-to-body ratios of any dinosaur, earning it a reputation as one of the 'smartest' dinosaurs. It was first named from a single distinctive tooth.
interestingFacts: Had one of the largest brain-to-body-size ratios of any known dinosaur.
Its large, forward-facing eyes hint at sharp vision, perhaps for low-light hunting.
Originally named in 1856 from just one small, saw-edged tooth.

meaning: after Quetzalcoatl, the Aztec feathered serpent
imageAttribution: Dmitry Bogdanov, Wikimedia Commons, Public domain
description: One of the largest flying animals of all time — a giant azhdarchid pterosaur with a wingspan of around 10–11 metres, standing as tall as a giraffe. It likely strode across the land stalking small prey before launching into powered flight. A pterosaur, not a dinosaur.
interestingFacts: Among the largest animals ever to fly, with a ~10–11 m wingspan.
Stood as tall as a giraffe and may have foraged on foot before taking off.
Named after Quetzalcoatl, the Aztec feathered-serpent god.

imageAttribution: Dmitry Bogdanov, Wikimedia Commons, Public domain
description: A long-tailed Jurassic pterosaur with a diamond-shaped skin vane at the tip of its tail and a mouthful of forward-pointing teeth for snatching fish. Exquisite specimens come from the Solnhofen limestone. A pterosaur, not a dinosaur.
interestingFacts: Its long tail ended in a diamond-shaped skin vane that likely acted as a rudder.
Forward-angled teeth were perfect for grabbing slippery fish.
Known from beautifully preserved Solnhofen fossils, some with skin traces.

imageAttribution: Dmitry Bogdanov, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 3.0
description: A giant marine lizard and apex predator of the Late Cretaceous seas, with powerful double-hinged jaws, a streamlined body and paddle-like limbs. One of the last and largest mosasaurs. A marine reptile, not a dinosaur.
interestingFacts: A huge sea-going lizard — not a dinosaur — that ruled the Late Cretaceous oceans.
Double-hinged jaws and extra teeth on the palate helped it grip large prey.
Among the first fossil reptiles ever recognised by science, back in the 1700s.

imageAttribution: Nobu Tamura, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.5
description: A colossal short-necked pliosaur with an enormous head and stout conical teeth — among the largest marine predators of the Early Cretaceous. It powered through the shallow sea that once flooded inland Australia. A marine reptile, not a dinosaur.
interestingFacts: A short-necked pliosaur whose skull alone was over 2 metres long.
Hunted the inland sea that once covered much of Australia.
Named after Kronos, leader of the Greek Titans.

description: An extraordinarily long-necked plesiosaur whose neck held over 70 vertebrae and made up more than half its length. It cruised the Western Interior Seaway, plucking fish with needle-like teeth. Famously, Cope first reconstructed it with the skull on the wrong end. A marine reptile, not a dinosaur.
interestingFacts: Its neck contained over 70 vertebrae — among the longest of any animal.
The neck alone made up more than half of its ~10 m length.
Edward Cope first assembled the skeleton with the head on the tail by mistake.

imageAttribution: Fred Wierum, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0
description: The largest raptor known — a powerfully built dromaeosaur with a sickle-shaped killing claw up to 23 cm long on each foot. It hunted Early Cretaceous North America tens of millions of years before smaller cousins like Velociraptor.
interestingFacts: By far the biggest raptor known, dwarfing Velociraptor.
Each foot carried a sickle claw up to about 23 cm long.
Named for Utah, where it was discovered in 1991.

imageAttribution: Connor Ashbridge, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0
description: A large spinosaurid with a long, crocodile-like snout full of conical teeth and a low sail along its back. It fished the rivers of Early Cretaceous Africa, much like its relatives Baryonyx and Spinosaurus.
interestingFacts: Its long, narrow snout worked like a crocodile's for snatching fish.
A low sail ran along its back on tall spine extensions.
Unearthed in the Sahara of Niger by Paul Sereno's team.

description: A sleek tyrannosaur from Late Cretaceous North America — a lighter, faster cousin of Tyrannosaurus that preyed on horned and duck-billed dinosaurs. It is known from many superb, complete skeletons.
interestingFacts: A lighter, faster relative of Tyrannosaurus rex.
Among the best-known tyrannosaurs, from many complete Canadian skeletons.
Youngsters had longer legs, likely for chasing swift prey.

imageAttribution: Emily Willoughby, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0
description: An armoured nodosaur studded with bony plates and rows of tall spikes along its neck and shoulders, but with no tail club. It grazed low plants across Early Cretaceous North America, relying on that spiky armour for defence.
interestingFacts: Bore rows of large defensive spikes over its neck and shoulders.
A nodosaur — armoured, but lacking the ankylosaurid tail club.
Its heavy tail made up roughly half its total length.

imageAttribution: Smokeybjb / Paleocolour, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0
description: A mid-sized Jurassic sauropod from China with an unusually short neck and — remarkably — a small bony club on the tip of its tail, a rare weapon among the long-necks.
interestingFacts: One of very few sauropods with a bony tail club for defence.
Had a notably short neck for a sauropod.
Known from dozens of skeletons unearthed in Sichuan, China.

description: One of the earliest known dinosaurs — a small, lightly built runner from the Late Triassic of Argentina. Its mix of leaf-shaped and pointed teeth hints at an omnivorous diet right at the dinosaurs' origin.
interestingFacts: Among the oldest known dinosaurs, at about 231 million years old.
A mix of tooth shapes suggests it ate both plants and small animals.
Found in the 'Valley of the Moon' (Ischigualasto), Argentina.

description: An early therizinosaur from the feathered Jehol fauna of China, covered in shaggy down and long, stiff display feathers. A big-clawed plant-eater, it shows just how bird-like these odd dinosaurs were.
interestingFacts: Clothed in downy feathers plus long, stiff filaments for display.
An early, small relative of the giant-clawed Therizinosaurus.
From China's Jehol Biota, famed for feathered dinosaurs.

imageAttribution: Jordan Mallon, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 2.5
description: A Middle Jurassic predator from China named for the single tall crest running along the top of its snout, most likely used for display. It is one of the better-known Jurassic theropods of Asia.
interestingFacts: Named for the single bony crest down the midline of its snout.
The hollow crest may have amplified calls or served for display.
One of few well-known Middle Jurassic theropods from China.

description: One of the largest mosasaurs — a giant marine lizard with a stiff, bony snout it may have used to ram prey. It patrolled the Western Interior Seaway eating fish, sharks, seabirds and even other mosasaurs. A marine reptile, not a dinosaur.
interestingFacts: One of the biggest mosasaurs, reaching around 13 metres.
Its bony snout-ram may have been used to stun prey.
Stomach contents show it ate fish, sharks and even other mosasaurs.

description: A dolphin-shaped ichthyosaur famous for its enormous eyes — among the largest of any animal — ideal for hunting squid in deep, dark water. Like other ichthyosaurs it gave birth to live young at sea. A marine reptile, not a dinosaur.
interestingFacts: Had some of the largest eyes of any animal, up to ~23 cm across.
Those huge eyes suited hunting in deep, dark water.
Gave birth to live young in the open sea.

imageAttribution: El fosilmaníaco, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0
description: A powerful short-necked pliosaur that hunted the Jurassic seas of Europe with a massive head and dagger-like teeth. Wildly oversized in documentaries, it was still a formidable ~6–7 m apex predator. A marine reptile, not a dinosaur.
interestingFacts: A short-necked pliosaur and apex predator of Jurassic European seas.
Famously exaggerated to 25 m on TV — really about 6–7 m long.
May have tracked prey underwater using a keen sense of smell.

description: The largest sea turtle ever known — over 4 metres from flipper to flipper — with a leathery shell of bony struts instead of a solid plate. It cruised the Western Interior Seaway feeding on jellyfish and shellfish. A marine reptile, not a dinosaur.
interestingFacts: The largest sea turtle ever found, over 4 m across the flippers.
Its shell was a framework of bony struts under leathery skin, not a solid dome.
Likely fed on jellyfish and shellfish in the Cretaceous seaway.

imageAttribution: Matt Martyniuk, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0
description: A fish-eating pterosaur with rounded crests on both its upper and lower jaws and a wingspan around 4.5 metres. It skimmed the seas over Cretaceous Brazil, snatching fish with interlocking teeth. A pterosaur, not a dinosaur.
interestingFacts: Had rounded keel-crests on both its upper and lower jaws.
Snatched fish from the sea surface with interlocking teeth.
Its name means 'old devil', after a spirit in Brazilian folklore.

imageAttribution: Dmitry Bogdanov (crest fixed by FunkMonk), Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 3.0
description: A small toothless pterosaur bearing an extraordinary antler-like head crest — a huge L-shaped structure that may have carried a sail of skin. It soared over the Late Cretaceous seas of North America. A pterosaur, not a dinosaur.
interestingFacts: Sported a giant antler-shaped head crest, perhaps with a skin sail.
Its toothless jaws were suited to snatching fish in flight.
Lacked the wing-finger claws that most other pterosaurs had.

imageAttribution: El fosilmaníaco, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0
description: A large fish-eating pterosaur with a keeled crest at the tip of its snout, known from the Cretaceous of England. Made famous — and greatly oversized — as the giant migrating flyer in Walking with Dinosaurs. A pterosaur, not a dinosaur.
interestingFacts: Bore a rounded keel-crest on the very tip of its snout.
Starred as the giant migrating pterosaur in Walking with Dinosaurs.
Its on-screen size was exaggerated; a ~5 m wingspan is likelier.

description: A sail-backed ornithopod from Early Cretaceous Africa. The tall spines along its back may have carried a display sail, helped control its temperature, or supported a fatty hump like a bison's. It cropped plants with a broad, duck-like beak.
interestingFacts: Tall back spines may have formed a sail or a fatty, bison-like hump.
A relative of Iguanodon with a broad beak for cropping plants.
Roamed the lush river deltas of Early Cretaceous Niger.

description: The first dinosaur found with clear evidence of feathers — a small compsognathid from China's Jehol Biota covered in simple downy filaments. Preserved pigments even reveal it had a ginger-and-white banded tail.
interestingFacts: The first dinosaur discovered with unmistakable feather traces.
Fossilised pigments show it had a ginger-and-white striped tail.
One of the smallest dinosaurs known, about the size of a turkey.

imageAttribution: Emily Willoughby, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0
description: A large-winged dromaeosaur from China preserved with big, layered wing feathers — despite being far too heavy to fly. It hints that many raptors wore bird-like wings for display or brooding rather than flight.
interestingFacts: Preserved with large, complex wing feathers although it couldn't fly.
A close cousin of Velociraptor, but bulkier and even more bird-like.
Suggests raptor wings first evolved for display or brooding, not flight.

description: The largest known duck-billed dinosaur — a colossal hadrosaur from China that rivalled the big meat-eaters in size. It grazed in herds, grinding tough plants with batteries of hundreds of teeth.
interestingFacts: The largest hadrosaur (duck-bill) known, up to ~15 metres long.
Its jaws held well over a thousand tightly packed grinding teeth.
One of the biggest animals of Late Cretaceous Asia.

description: An ostrich-like ornithomimid with a toothless beak, long legs and grasping hands. A fast runner of Late Cretaceous North America, it likely fed on plants, insects and small animals.
interestingFacts: Built like an ostrich, and probably just as fleet-footed.
Its toothless beak suited an omnivorous diet.
Long-fingered hands may have raked in plants or small prey.

description: One of the largest raptors — a heavily built dromaeosaur from Mongolia with a big sickle claw on each foot. Its name nods to Achilles, for the powerful ankle tendons that anchored its leg muscles.
interestingFacts: Among the largest raptors, rivalling Utahraptor in bulk.
Named after Achilles, for its powerful ankle tendons.
A robust, heavyset hunter rather than a swift lightweight.

description: A long-snouted tyrannosaur nicknamed 'Pinocchio rex' for its slender, elongated snout — quite unlike the deep jaws of T. rex. It likely chased smaller, quicker prey across Late Cretaceous Asia.
interestingFacts: Nicknamed 'Pinocchio rex' for its unusually long, slim snout.
Its narrow jaws suited catching smaller, faster prey than T. rex.
Confirmed long-snouted tyrannosaurs were a real group, not just juveniles.

description: A small, lightly built predator from the Late Jurassic of North America with a short skull and grasping hands. It likely darted through the undergrowth hunting lizards, mammals and hatchlings.
interestingFacts: A small, agile hunter of the Late Jurassic Morrison ecosystem.
Its name 'bird robber' reflects an early idea that it raided nests.
Grasping three-fingered hands helped it seize small prey.

description: A Chinese stegosaur with two rows of tall, pointed plates and a spiked tail. It browsed low vegetation in the Late Jurassic forests of Sichuan.
interestingFacts: Bore tall, pointed plates rather than the broad ones of Stegosaurus.
Its spiked tail — a 'thagomizer' — was a formidable defensive weapon.
One of the best-known stegosaurs from China.

imageAttribution: Nobu Tamura, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 3.0
description: An early sauropodomorph from Early Jurassic southern Africa that walked on two legs and browsed plants with a small head on a long neck. Nests of its eggs and embryos are among the oldest known.
interestingFacts: An early relative of the giant sauropods, but only about 4 m long.
Fossil nests preserve some of the oldest known dinosaur embryos.
Walked on two legs despite its long-necked, plant-eating build.

description: An early long-necked sauropodomorph from China — and the first complete dinosaur skeleton ever mounted in the country. It browsed vegetation and may have used thumb claws for defence.
interestingFacts: The first complete dinosaur skeleton mounted in China.
An early cousin of the giant sauropods, standing semi-upright.
Its embryos yielded some of the oldest dinosaur proteins ever found.

description: One of the largest predators of Late Triassic Europe — a slender, crested theropod related to Coelophysis. It hunted early plant-eaters across what is now Germany.
interestingFacts: One of the largest meat-eaters of Late Triassic Europe.
A slender, fast coelophysoid, likely with twin crests on its snout.
Named after the collector who found it, Hugo Rühle von Lilienstern.

description: A large, bulky sauropodomorph from Late Triassic Argentina — one of the biggest land animals of its day. Its heavy, column-like legs suggest it walked on all fours, foreshadowing the giant sauropods to come.
interestingFacts: One of the largest land animals of the Late Triassic, up to ~10 m.
Its sturdy, pillar-like legs hint that it walked on all fours.
An early forerunner of the giant long-necked sauropods.

imageAttribution: Connor Ashbridge, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0
description: A small Chinese stegosaur with a mix of thick plates and spikes down its back — narrower and more spike-like than Stegosaurus — plus a spiked tail for defence.
interestingFacts: A small stegosaur with narrow, spike-like plates along its back.
Defended itself with a spiked, club-like tail.
Shared its Late Jurassic home with Tuojiangosaurus.

imageAttribution: Nobu Tamura, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 3.0
description: The earliest and most primitive known horned dinosaur — a small, two-legged plant-eater from Late Jurassic China. Long before Triceratops, it shows how the ceratopsian lineage began.
interestingFacts: The oldest and most primitive known ceratopsian (horned dinosaur).
Small and two-legged, with only the first hints of a frill.
Its name 'hidden dragon' nods to the film Crouching Tiger, Hidden Dragon.

imageAttribution: Dmitry Bogdanov, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0
description: A crested pterosaur from Cretaceous Brazil famous for its enormous head crest — a bony frame that likely supported a huge sail of skin, probably for display. A pterosaur, not a dinosaur.
interestingFacts: Sported one of the largest head crests of any pterosaur.
The bony crest likely framed a big sail of skin for display.
Named after Tupã, a thunder god of Tupi mythology.

imageAttribution: Petr Menshikov, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0
description: A filter-feeding pterosaur with hundreds of long, bristle-like teeth in its upturned lower jaw, used to strain tiny creatures from the water much like a flamingo. A pterosaur, not a dinosaur.
interestingFacts: Had around a thousand fine, bristle-like teeth for filter-feeding.
Strained plankton and small crustaceans from water like a flamingo.
Its curved lower jaw held the comb of filtering teeth.

description: One of the earliest known pterosaurs, from the Late Triassic of Italy. Its jaws held multi-cusped teeth of several shapes for gripping fish, and it had a long tail tipped with a small vane. A pterosaur, not a dinosaur.
interestingFacts: Among the earliest known pterosaurs, from the Late Triassic.
Had over a hundred teeth of several shapes for catching fish.
Its long tail ended in a small diamond-shaped vane.

imageAttribution: Dmitry Bogdanov, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0
description: A small long-tailed pterosaur from Late Jurassic Kazakhstan — famous as one of the first pterosaurs shown to be covered in hair-like 'pycnofibres', proving these flyers were furry and warm-bodied. A pterosaur, not a dinosaur.
interestingFacts: One of the first pterosaurs found covered in hair-like fibres.
Showed that pterosaurs were fuzzy and probably warm-blooded.
Its name means 'hairy filth' or 'hairy devil'.

imageAttribution: Dmitry Bogdanov, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 3.0
description: A gigantic Triassic ichthyosaur — one of the largest marine reptiles ever, reaching around 15 metres. Dozens of skeletons lie together at one Nevada site, and it is now the state fossil. A marine reptile, not a dinosaur.
interestingFacts: One of the largest ichthyosaurs, at around 15 metres long.
Dozens died together at a single Nevada site, now a state park.
It is the state fossil of Nevada.

imageAttribution: Dmitry Bogdanov, Wikimedia Commons, Public domain
description: A huge Early Jurassic ichthyosaur with some of the largest eyes of any animal — up to 20 cm across — for hunting in deep water. Among the first giant ichthyosaurs found, by pioneering fossil hunter Mary Anning. A marine reptile, not a dinosaur.
interestingFacts: Had eyes up to ~20 cm wide, among the largest of any animal.
One of the first giant ichthyosaurs, found by Mary Anning as a girl.
A powerful deep-water hunter of the Early Jurassic seas.

imageAttribution: Dmitry Bogdanov, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0
description: A colossal short-necked pliosaur — an apex predator of the Late Jurassic seas with a skull up to 2 metres long and crushing teeth. Some species rank among the most powerful marine predators ever known. A marine reptile, not a dinosaur.
interestingFacts: A short-necked pliosaur with a skull up to 2 metres long.
Its bite may have been among the most powerful of any animal.
Prowled the Late Jurassic seas as an apex predator.

imageAttribution: Dmitry Bogdanov, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 3.0
description: A medium-sized, long-necked plesiosaur from the Middle Jurassic with slender, needle-like teeth that meshed into a trap for catching small fish and squid. A marine reptile, not a dinosaur.
interestingFacts: Its fine, interlocking teeth formed a trap for small fish and squid.
A moderately long-necked plesiosaur of the Middle Jurassic seas.
Well known from many complete skeletons found in England.

description: A therizinosaur from Late Cretaceous North America — a pot-bellied, feathered plant-eater that stood upright with a small head, long neck and huge hand claws. It was the first therizinosaur found in the Americas.
interestingFacts: The first therizinosaur ('scythe lizard') found in the Americas.
A big-bellied, feathered plant-eater despite its fearsome claws.
Its long claws likely pulled down branches rather than caught prey.

description: A mid-sized ankylosaur from the Gobi Desert, armoured with bony plates and wielding a bony club at the end of its tail. Many juveniles have been found together, hinting that the young may have lived in groups.
interestingFacts: Armoured all over, with a bony club at the tip of its tail.
Herds of juveniles have been found together in the Gobi Desert.
Had small extra openings in its skull whose purpose is still debated.

imageAttribution: Nobu Tamura, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 2.5
description: A stout little ornithopod that was among the very last dinosaurs before the mass extinction. Built for browsing low plants, it had a bulky body and strong hind legs for running from predators.
interestingFacts: One of the last dinosaurs alive before the end-Cretaceous extinction.
A stocky plant-eater built for running on strong hind legs.
Its name 'wonderful lizard' reflects the fine skeleton first found.

description: A tiny, bird-like raptor from Montana with a surprisingly large brain and long grasping arms. Known from a beautifully preserved juvenile skeleton, it hints at how sharp small dromaeosaurs may have been.
interestingFacts: A crow-sized raptor, among the smallest known.
Had an unusually large brain for a dinosaur of its size.
Found by a 14-year-old boy hiking in Montana in 1995.

description: A bizarre island-dwelling raptor from Cretaceous Romania with a stocky build and TWO sickle claws on each foot instead of one. It evolved its strange features in isolation on a prehistoric island.
interestingFacts: Had two enlarged sickle claws on each foot, not the usual one.
Evolved its stocky, unusual body in isolation on a Cretaceous island.
Its name means 'stocky dragon', after a dragon of Romanian folklore.

imageAttribution: Danielle Dufault, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0
description: A horned dinosaur from Canada with a spectacular frill rimmed by curled, hook-like hornlets and a tall nose horn. It is one of the oldest ceratopsids known to sport a prominent nasal horn.
interestingFacts: Its frill was lined with distinctive forward-curling hornlets.
Named after fossil hunter Wendy Sloboda, who found it.
Among the earliest horned dinosaurs with a tall nose horn.

description: A horned dinosaur nicknamed 'Hellboy' for the two stubby horns over its eyes and its crown-like frill studded with plates. It shows a chasmosaurine that evolved a centrosaurine-style frill — a striking case of convergent evolution.
interestingFacts: Nicknamed 'Hellboy' for its stubby brow horns and crown-like frill.
Its ornate frill mimicked those of a different ceratopsian group.
Discovered by geologist Peter Hews along a Canadian riverbank.

description: A large horned dinosaur with one of the biggest skulls of any land animal — a huge frill plus a nose horn and two long brow horns. Its name means 'five-horned face', counting the extra spikes on its cheeks.
interestingFacts: Had one of the largest skulls of any land animal, frill included.
Its name counts two extra hornlets on the cheeks as 'horns'.
Roamed the Late Cretaceous of what is now New Mexico.

imageAttribution: Connor Ashbridge, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0
description: A duck-billed dinosaur from China famous for the tall, forward-pointing hollow crest on its head — long nicknamed the 'unicorn dinosaur'. The crest likely amplified its calls or served for display.
interestingFacts: Nicknamed the 'unicorn dinosaur' for its tall, upright head crest.
The hollow crest may have amplified calls or aided display.
One of the few crested hadrosaurs known from China.

imageAttribution: Connor Ashbridge, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0
description: A crested, duck-billed dinosaur of Late Cretaceous North America with a rounded, hollow head crest and tall spines along its back. Nests, eggs and embryos have revealed how quickly its young grew.
interestingFacts: Sported a rounded, hollow crest likely used to make sounds.
Fossil embryos show its babies grew remarkably fast.
Tall back spines gave it a slightly ridged silhouette.

description: One of the first armoured dinosaurs ever named — a club-less nodosaur covered in rows of bony knobs and plates set in a banded, 'woven' pattern that inspired its species name textilis.
interestingFacts: Among the first armoured dinosaurs named, back in 1889.
Its bony armour formed a regular, woven-looking pattern.
A nodosaur — armoured, but with no tail club.

description: A small, crestless oviraptorid from Mongolia with a stout, toothless beak. Its name reflects an old idea that it cracked open shellfish, though it likely ate a varied diet.
interestingFacts: A small oviraptorid with a powerful, toothless beak but no crest.
Its name 'conch thief' reflects a theory that it ate shellfish.
A close relative of the crested, egg-brooding Oviraptor.

imageAttribution: Danny Cicchetti, Wikimedia Commons, CC BY-SA 4.0
description: A feathered oviraptorosaur from China crowned with a tall, helmet-like crest strikingly similar to a modern cassowary's — likely used for display and to signal maturity.
interestingFacts: Wore a tall casque crest much like a living cassowary's.
The crest probably signalled maturity and helped it show off.
Known from a well-preserved skeleton found in southern China.

description: A bizarre little raptor with a swan-like neck, a duck-like snout full of tiny teeth, and flipper-like arms — apparently a semi-aquatic dinosaur that swam after fish, unlike any other known raptor.
interestingFacts: A semi-aquatic raptor with a swan-like neck and flipper-like arms.
Its duck-like snout held dozens of tiny teeth for catching fish.
One of the strangest dinosaurs described this century.
